evidence.quote: Danville is set in a narrow section of the San Ramon Valley with the Las Trampas Ridge to the west and the Diablo Range to the east.

evidence.claim: Interstate 680 follows the San Ramon Valley through Contra Costa County, with local-road connections in San Ramon, Danville and Alamo before Walnut Creek.
evidence.quote: Upon entering Contra Costa County, the route meets numerous local roads through the cities of San Ramon, Danville, and Alamo before entering Walnut Creek, where it meets SR 24.

evidence.claim: At Danville, the valley narrows between Las Trampas Ridge and the Diablo Range, with Mount Diablo to the east.
evidence.quote: Danville is set in a narrow section of the San Ramon Valley with the Las Trampas Ridge to the west and the Diablo Range to the east. The most prominent landmark of Danville is the backdrop of Mount Diablo, which stands to the east

evidence.quote: The routing was very close to the present I-680, following such roads as Pleasanton Sunol Road, San Ramon Valley Boulevard, Danville Boulevard, Main Street in Walnut Creek, Contra Costa Boulevard, and Pacheco Boulevard.

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Public Roads approved the Bay Area interstate loop in 1955.
evidence.quote: The Bureau of Public Roads approved urban routes of the Interstate Highway System on September 15, 1955, including a loop around the San Francisco Bay, soon numbered I-280 and I-680.

evidence.claim: The freeway bypass of downtown Walnut Creek opened in 1960, connecting with SR 24 toward Oakland.
evidence.quote: A southerly extension, bypassing downtown Walnut Creek to South Main Street, opened on March 22, 1960, connecting with the SR 24 freeway to Oakland.

evidence.quote: The Iron Horse Regional Trail runs through Danville. It was first a railroad that has been converted to a 10-foot-wide (3.0 m) path that consists of biking and hiking trails as well as controlled intersections.

evidence.claim: At Alamo Elementary School, the courtyard holds a bell from the 1880s, even though the school itself opened in 1965.
evidence.quote: Today's Alamo Elementary School at 100 Wilson Road opened in 1965. It is the fourth Alamo school bearing the name. It has the original school bell from the 1880s in its courtyard.

evidence.claim: It is the fourth school to bear the Alamo name; the first was built in 1871.
evidence.quote: The first Alamo school was built back in 1871.

evidence.claim: Mary Ann and John Jones passed through Alamo in 1847 and returned in 1851.
evidence.quote: Pioneers Mary Ann and John Jones traveled through Alamo in 1847.

evidence.claim: returned in 1851.
evidence.quote: The Jones family returned to Alamo in 1851

evidence.claim: John became the first postmaster in 1852, while Mary Ann worked on schooling children and starting a Cumberland Presbyterian church.
evidence.quote: John became the first postmaster in 1852 and she applied her considerable energies to schooling children and beginning a Cumberland Presbyterian church.

evidence.claim: A San Ramon Valley Historical Society plaque accompanies the bell, commemorating early education in Alamo.
evidence.quote: The bell has a San Ramon Valley Historical Society plaque that commemorates the history of early education in Alamo.

evidence.claim: The three earlier Alamo schools stood near the present corner of Stone Valley Road West and Danville Boulevard.
evidence.quote: The three previous Alamo Schools were built near what is today the corner of Stone Valley Road West and Danville Boulevard.

evidence.claim: Eugene O'Neill used his 1936 Nobel Prize money to build Tao House above Danville.
evidence.quote: Eugene O'Neill had won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1936, and used the prize money to build what he named Tao House above Danville.

evidence.claim: He and his wife, actress Carlotta Monterey, designed the two-story house themselves and lived there from 1937 to 1944.
evidence.quote: O'Neill and his wife, actress Carlotta Monterey, showed their interest in Asian art, decor, and thought in preparing the home. The two personally designed the two-story, three-bedroom home from the ground up.

evidence.claim: lived there from 1937 to 1944.
evidence.quote: O'Neill and his wife lived in the home from 1937 to 1944.

evidence.claim: Here he wrote The Iceman Cometh and Long Day's Journey Into Night.
evidence.quote: At this home, O'Neill wrote his final plays: The Iceman Cometh, Long Day's Journey Into Night, Hughie, and A Moon for the Misbegotten.

evidence.claim: The house faced demolition in the early 1970s; women including Darlene Blair and Lois Sizoo formed the Eugene O'Neill Foundation to raise money to buy it.
evidence.quote: The house was saved from demolition in the early 1970s. Several women formed the Eugene O’Neill Foundation, including president Darlene Blair and executive vice president Lois Sizoo, in order to raise money to buy Tao House

evidence.claim: National Park Service management followed in 1980.
evidence.quote: passed into the management of the National Park Service in 1980.

evidence.claim: The foundation maintains an archive at the house, including manuscripts, photographs and the playwright’s original phonograph record collection.
evidence.quote: The Foundation maintains an archive of Eugene O'Neill-related material at Tao House (including photographs, playbills, manuscripts, posters, and O'Neill's original phonograph record collection)

evidence.claim: Private vehicles are not allowed at Tao House.
evidence.quote: Private vehicles are not allowed.

evidence.claim: The Museum of the San Ramon Valley occupies the restored 1891 Southern Pacific depot.
evidence.quote: Museum of the San Ramon Valley (located in the restored 1891 Southern Pacific depot)

evidence.claim: The railroad changed both farming and the shape of town: growers shifted from wheat to fruit and nuts after the spur arrived in 1891.
evidence.quote: Initially a farming community, the Town of Danville switched from wheat to fruits and nuts after the Southern Pacific Railroad built a spur line through the area in 1891.

evidence.claim: John Hartz sold land for the depot, then subdivided lots east of the station, shifting the town's focus from Front Street to Hartz Avenue.
evidence.quote: John Hartz sold 8.65 acres (3.50 ha) of his land for the Danville Depot and granted land access to the station. He then subdivided and sold lots east of the station, shifting the town's focus from Front Street to Hartz Avenue.

evidence.claim: The Danville Hotel was moved to face Hartz Avenue in 1927.
evidence.quote: The Danville Hotel originally sat across from the station and was moved to face Hartz Avenue in 1927.

evidence.claim: Passenger service ended in 1934; freight trains continued through town until the line was abandoned in 1978.
evidence.quote: Passenger service ended in 1934. The Southern Pacific Railroad trains continued to pass through town with freight until 1978 when the line was abandoned.

evidence.claim: The former railway through town now carries the Iron Horse Regional Trail.
evidence.quote: The Iron Horse Regional Trail runs through Danville. It was first a railroad
